title: System Calls, Interrupts & I/O
tagline: How programs cross into the kernel, how hardware gets the CPU's attention, and how I/O scales from blocking reads to epoll and io_uring

sections.content:
Your program cannot touch the disk, the network card, the screen, or even another process's memory. Not directly. Every one of those actions goes through a narrow, heavily guarded doorway into the operating-system kernel called a **system call**. When Node.js reads a file, when Python opens a socket, when your shell starts `ls`, the CPU stops running your code, switches into a privileged mode, runs kernel code on your behalf, and then switches back. A busy server can cross that boundary hundreds of thousands of times a second. Starting Node.js and reading one small file takes well over a thousand system calls.

Going the other way are **interrupts**: the hardware's way of tapping the CPU on the shoulder. A network packet arrived. A disk finished a transfer. The timer fired, so the scheduler can take the CPU back from a thread that won't let go. Interrupts are why your machine can wait for a thousand slow devices without checking each one in a loop, and why one runaway loop can't freeze the whole system.

Between these two mechanisms sits **I/O**, the part of almost every real application that is slow. This chapter follows the full path: user mode and kernel mode, what physically happens when you execute the `syscall` instruction, why a syscall costs roughly a hundred times more than a function call (and how the vDSO avoids some of them), how `strace` lets you watch every call, how interrupts, exceptions, and traps differ, how drivers split work into top and bottom halves, how DMA moves data without the CPU, and how I/O grew from blocking `read()` through `select`, `poll`, `epoll`, and `kqueue` to `io_uring`.

We finish with something you use every day: how Node.js and libuv combine non-blocking sockets, an `epoll`/`kqueue` event loop, and a thread pool so that one JavaScript thread can serve thousands of connections. You will also see where that design quietly blocks.

sections.title: The Bank Teller Window
sections.content:
Picture a bank. Customers (user programs) wait in the lobby. The vault, the ledgers, and the cash drawers (hardware, kernel memory, other customers' accounts) are behind bulletproof glass. Customers cannot walk into the vault, however politely they ask.

To get anything done, a customer goes to the **teller window** (the system-call interface) and hands over a form with a **transaction code** (the syscall number) and details (the arguments): "withdraw, account 42, $100." The teller (kernel) **checks** the form: is this your account, is the amount sane, is the pointer you gave me really yours? Then the teller does the work behind the glass and slides back a result or an error code. The customer never touched the vault.

Some requests take a while: "wire this money abroad" (disk or network I/O). A **blocking** customer stands at the window until it's done. A **non-blocking** customer takes a ticket and leaves. An **epoll** customer hands in fifty tickets and asks, "wake me when any of these are ready." An **io_uring** customer drops a stack of forms in a tray and later picks up finished receipts from another tray, without queueing at the window for each one.

Meanwhile the bank's alarm bells are **interrupts**. When the armoured truck arrives (a disk transfer completes), the bell rings, a teller briefly stops serving the queue to sign for the delivery (the top half), and the slow job of counting the cash is left for later (the bottom half).

sections.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode: Privilege Rings
sections.content:
Modern CPUs enforce **privilege levels** in hardware. On x86 these are **rings 0–3**. Ring 0 is fully privileged; ring 3 is the most restricted. Mainstream operating systems use only two of them: the **kernel runs in ring 0** and **applications run in ring 3** (rings 1 and 2 are effectively unused, and hypervisors get their own "root mode" via VT-x/AMD-V). ARM calls these **exception levels**: EL0 for applications, EL1 for the kernel, EL2 for a hypervisor, EL3 for secure firmware.

What the CPU refuses to do in user mode:
- **Privileged instructions**: changing the page-table root (`CR3`), disabling interrupts (`cli`), talking to I/O ports, reloading the interrupt table. Trying one raises a *general protection fault* and the kernel kills the process.
- **Touching kernel memory**: every page-table entry has a user/supervisor bit. A ring-3 access to a supervisor page faults.
- **Touching other processes' memory**: their pages simply aren't mapped in your page tables.

This is what makes a process a sandbox. A bug in your code can corrupt *your* memory and crash *your* process, but it can't overwrite the kernel or another program. The cost is that **every interaction with the outside world must ask the kernel**, and asking means a controlled, hardware-assisted switch from ring 3 to ring 0 and back.

There are exactly three ways the CPU enters the kernel:
1. **System calls**: the program deliberately asks (`syscall` on x86-64, `svc` on ARM64).
2. **Exceptions**: the current instruction caused a problem (page fault, divide by zero, invalid opcode).
3. **Hardware interrupts**: a device or timer needs attention, unrelated to the instruction that happened to be running.

In all three cases the CPU saves enough state to resume, switches to a kernel stack, and jumps to a kernel-chosen entry point. User code never chooses where in the kernel execution begins. That rule is the whole security model.

sections.title: Anatomy of a System Call: From write() to the Kernel and Back
sections.content:
Follow `write(1, "hi\n", 3)` on x86-64 Linux:

1. **Your code calls the libc wrapper** `write()`, an ordinary function call.
2. **The wrapper loads registers by convention**: the syscall number goes in `rax` (`write` is 1 on x86-64), the arguments in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, then `r10`, `r8`, `r9` for up to six. Then it executes the single instruction **`syscall`**.
3. **The CPU switches mode in hardware**: it saves the user instruction pointer in `rcx` and the flags in `r11`, switches to ring 0, and jumps to the address the kernel stored at boot in the `IA32_LSTAR` model-specific register (Linux's `entry_SYSCALL_64`). The CPU does *not* switch stacks; the entry code does that first (`swapgs`, load the per-CPU kernel stack). If Meltdown mitigation (KPTI) is on, it also switches to the kernel page tables.
4. **The kernel saves user registers** in a `pt_regs` frame, checks the number, and indexes the **syscall table**: `sys_call_table[1]` leads to `ksys_write()` and then `vfs_write()`.
5. **It validates everything**: is fd 1 open and writable, does the buffer really lie in user memory? Copying from user memory uses `copy_from_user()`, which survives a bad pointer by returning `-EFAULT` instead of crashing the kernel.
6. **The work happens**. This may finish immediately (copy into the page cache or a pipe buffer), or the thread may **sleep** on a wait queue until a device is ready. Meanwhile the scheduler runs something else.
7. **Return**: the result goes in `rax` and `sysret` (or `iret`) drops back to ring 3 at the saved instruction. On failure the kernel returns a small negative number (`-EBADF` is −9); the libc wrapper turns that into `return -1` plus `errno = EBADF`.

Other architectures differ only in detail. ARM64 uses `svc #0` with the number in `x8` and arguments in `x0`–`x5`. 32-bit x86 used the slow `int 0x80` software interrupt, and later `sysenter`. The principle is the same everywhere: **a numbered request, arguments in registers, one trapping instruction, a fixed kernel entry point.**

Linux on x86-64 has roughly 460 syscall numbers. The numbers are a **stable ABI**: Linux never renumbers a syscall and almost never removes one, which is why a statically linked binary from 2005 still runs today. macOS is the opposite. Its syscall numbers are private and can change between releases, and Apple supports only calls made through `libSystem`. That is one reason Go switched to calling libc on macOS.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as App code (ring 3)
    participant Libc as libc write()
    participant CPU as CPU
    participant K as Kernel (ring 0)
    participant Dev as Driver / page cache
    App->>Libc: write(fd, buf, n)
    Libc->>CPU: rax=1, rdi=fd, rsi=buf, rdx=n, then syscall
    CPU->>K: save rip/rflags, ring 0, jump to entry_SYSCALL_64
    K->>K: switch stack, save pt_regs, sys_call_table[1]
    K->>Dev: vfs_write - validate fd, copy_from_user
    Dev-->>K: bytes accepted (or sleep until ready)
    K-->>CPU: rax = result, sysret
    CPU-->>Libc: back in ring 3
    Libc-->>App: return n, or -1 with errno set
sections.caption: One `write()` call: the libc wrapper loads registers and executes `syscall`. The CPU switches to ring 0 at a fixed entry point. The kernel dispatches through the syscall table, validates the user's pointers, does or schedules the work, and returns. A negative kernel return value becomes `-1` plus `errno` in libc.

sections.title: What a Syscall Really Costs, and How the vDSO Avoids It
sections.content:
A function call costs about a nanosecond. A minimal syscall like `getpid()` on a modern x86 server costs **on the order of 50–100 ns without security mitigations, and a few hundred nanoseconds with them**. That's roughly two orders of magnitude more. Where does the time go?

- **Direct cost**: the mode switch, saving and restoring registers, the entry and exit code, argument checking.
- **Mitigation cost**: after Meltdown and Spectre (2018), kernels switch page tables on entry and exit (**KPTI**), clear CPU buffers, and harden indirect branches. PCID tags soften the TLB flush, but workloads heavy in syscalls saw 5–30% slowdowns in 2018.
- **Indirect cost**: kernel code and data evict your program's lines from the L1/L2 caches, TLB, and branch predictors. When you return, your code runs slower for a while. The FlexSC paper (OSDI 2010) measured user-mode instructions-per-cycle staying depressed for thousands of cycles after a single syscall.

Two big lessons follow. First, **batch**: one `write()` of 64 KB is vastly cheaper than 65,536 one-byte writes. This is why stdio and Node streams buffer, why `writev()`/`readv()` exist, why databases group commits, and why `io_uring` can submit dozens of operations with one kernel entry. Second, **some "syscalls" don't need the kernel at all**.

That second trick is the **vDSO** (virtual dynamic shared object). At `exec` time the kernel maps a tiny shared library, `linux-vdso.so.1`, into every process, together with a read-only data page that the kernel keeps updated. Functions like `clock_gettime()`, `gettimeofday()`, `time()`, and `getcpu()` are implemented *in user space* inside the vDSO. They read the kernel-maintained clock data plus the CPU's timestamp counter, with no ring switch. Linux 6.11 (2024) added `getrandom()` to the vDSO too, so fast user-space random numbers no longer need a kernel entry (glibc 2.41+ uses it). This is why `performance.now()`, `process.hrtime()`, and `time.monotonic()` are cheap enough to call in hot loops. Run `ldd /bin/ls` and you'll see `linux-vdso.so.1` listed with no file path: it isn't on disk.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Same bytes, two strategies. Each `fs.writeSync()` call is one `write()` syscall. Measured on a 2021 laptop and in a Linux container (Node 22), 200,000 one-byte writes took about **0.5–0.6 s, roughly 2.5–3 µs per call**, including Node's JS-to-C++ binding and file-system work. A single 200 KB write took **under 1 ms, hundreds to thousands of times faster**. Your numbers will differ, but the ratio is always huge. Note the timer: `process.hrtime.bigint()` reads the clock through the vDSO on Linux (and the commpage on macOS), so timing doesn't add syscalls of its own. The lesson for production code: buffer small writes (streams, `writev`, batching log lines) instead of issuing one syscall per item.

sections.title: The System Calls You Actually Use
sections.content:
Every high-level API you know is a thin layer over a few dozen syscalls:

| Area | Syscalls | What you know them as |
|---|---|---|
| Files | `openat`, `read`, `write`, `pread64`, `close`, `lseek`, `statx`, `fsync` | `fs.readFile`, `open()` in Python |
| Memory | `mmap`, `munmap`, `mprotect`, `brk` | `malloc`, V8 heap growth, loading shared libraries |
| Processes | `clone`/`clone3`, `fork`, `execve`, `wait4`, `exit_group` | `child_process.spawn`, `subprocess.run`, threads |
| Networking | `socket`, `bind`, `listen`, `accept4`, `connect`, `sendto`, `recvfrom` | `net.createServer`, `requests.get` |
| Waiting | `epoll_wait`, `poll`, `futex`, `nanosleep` | event loops, mutexes, `sleep()` |
| Signals | `rt_sigaction`, `kill`, `rt_sigprocmask` | `process.on('SIGTERM')`, Ctrl-C |

A few deserve a closer look:
- **`open` is really `openat`**: modern glibc implements `open()` with `openat(AT_FDCWD, ...)`, which resolves paths relative to a directory fd and avoids race conditions. That is why `strace` shows `openat` everywhere.
- **`fork` is really `clone`**: on Linux, `fork()`, `vfork()`, and `pthread_create()` all call `clone`/`clone3` with different flags. A thread is `clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD | ...)`: a new task that shares the address space, file table, and signal handlers. A process is a `clone` that shares almost nothing (and copies memory lazily with copy-on-write).
- **`execve`** throws away the current memory image and loads a new program. Combined with `fork` it gives the Unix "fork then exec" model; `posix_spawn()` wraps both, often more efficiently.
- **`mmap`** maps files or anonymous memory into the address space. It's how the dynamic loader brings in libraries and how allocators get large blocks.
- **`futex`** ("fast user-space mutex") lets locks stay entirely in user space while uncontended and only enter the kernel to sleep or wake. That's why it dominates `strace -c` for multithreaded runtimes.

**libc wrappers** do more than load registers. They set `errno`, retry or report `EINTR`, add cancellation points for threads, pick the newest available syscall (`clone3` vs `clone`, `statx` vs `fstat`), and sometimes emulate calls in user space. Go and Zig skip libc and issue syscalls directly on Linux; on macOS, BSDs, and Windows, going through the system library is the only supported route.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# Linux. Watch every syscall Node.js makes to read one file.
$ cat read-file.js
const fs = require('fs');
const data = fs.readFileSync('/etc/os-release', 'utf8');
process.stdout.write(`read ${data.length} bytes\n`);

# -f follows threads, -e filters to the calls we care about
$ strace -f -e trace=openat,read,write,close node read-file.js 2>&1 | grep -A4 os-release
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/os-release", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 17
read(17, "NAME=\"Alpine Linux\"\nID=alpine\nVE"..., 8192) = 188
read(17, "", 8192)                      = 0        # 0 bytes = end of file
close(17)                               = 0
write(1, "read 188 bytes\n", 15)        = 15

# -c: a summary table instead of a log (Node 22, abridged)
$ strace -f -c node read-file.js
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
 69.98    0.307355        7317        42         5 futex        # threads waiting on each other
 16.98    0.074602       18650         4           epoll_pwait  # the event loop sleeping
  3.88    0.017051          42       398           munmap
  2.58    0.011353          28       398           mmap         # V8 heap + shared libraries
  0.87    0.003820         173        22           close
  0.49    0.002163         360         6           clone        # libuv pool + V8 worker threads
100.00    0.394452         287      1371        71 total        # ~1,400 syscalls for "read a file"

# Other useful forms
$ strace -p 1234 -e trace=network -T     # attach to a running PID, show time spent in each call
$ strace -e trace=%file python3 -c 'import json'   # every path Python probes while importing
sections.explanation: `strace` uses `ptrace` to stop the traced process at every syscall entry and exit and print the call, its decoded arguments, and its return value (output above captured in a Linux container with Node 22). Things to notice: `readFileSync` is just `openat` → `read` until it returns 0 → `close`. Errors show up as `= -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)`. And simply starting Node costs well over a thousand syscalls, mostly memory mapping and thread start-up. The per-call times are inflated because `ptrace` stops the process twice per syscall. That is why strace can slow a program **10–100×** and shouldn't be left attached to a busy production process. There, use `perf trace` or eBPF tools (`bpftrace`, `syscount`) instead. On macOS the equivalents are `dtruss` (needs SIP relaxed) and `fs_usage`.

sections.title: Interrupts, Exceptions, and Traps
sections.content:
The CPU has one mechanism for "stop what you're doing and run kernel code": the **interrupt descriptor table (IDT)** on x86 (the *vector table* on ARM), with one handler address per vector number (256 on x86). What differs is *who* raised the event and *when*:

**Hardware interrupts are asynchronous.** A device signals the CPU, completely unrelated to the instruction that's running. Old PCs had dedicated IRQ lines through a PIC; modern systems use the **APIC**, and PCIe devices raise **MSI/MSI-X** interrupts by writing a small message to a special memory address. An NVMe SSD or 100 GbE NIC can have one interrupt vector per queue, each steered to a different core. The **local APIC timer** is the most important interrupt of all: it is how the scheduler preempts a thread that never yields. CPUs also send each other **inter-processor interrupts (IPIs)**, for example "flush your TLB" or "reschedule."

**Exceptions are synchronous.** The current instruction caused them, so they always happen at the same place for the same input. Intel splits them into three kinds:
- **Faults** are reported *before* the instruction completes, and the CPU re-executes it after the handler returns. The **page fault** (vector 14) is the famous one: the kernel loads the missing page, returns, and the load instruction runs again as if nothing happened.
- **Traps** are reported *after* the instruction, and execution continues with the next one. Examples: the breakpoint instruction `int3` (how debuggers work) and single-step debugging.
- **Aborts** are unrecoverable: machine-check errors (failing hardware), double faults. The usual result is a kernel panic or a killed process.

**System calls** are deliberate, synchronous entries. Textbooks often call them "traps" or "software interrupts" because historically they were (`int 0x80` on Linux/i386, `int 0x2e` on Windows). Modern `syscall`/`svc` instructions use a dedicated fast path instead of the IDT, but conceptually they are still a trap: an intentional, synchronous transfer to the kernel.

Interrupts can be **masked** (temporarily disabled) by the kernel during critical sections. Non-maskable interrupts (NMIs) can't be masked; they're used for hardware errors, watchdogs, and profilers. Run `cat /proc/interrupts` on Linux to see per-CPU counts for every vector: timer, NVMe queues, NIC queues, IPIs.

sections.caption: Every entry into the kernel falls into one of these buckets. Hardware interrupts arrive asynchronously from devices. Everything else is synchronous to the current instruction: deliberate system calls, or exceptions. Exceptions are faults (retry the instruction), traps (continue after it), or aborts (no recovery).

sections.title: Interrupt Handlers: Top Halves and Bottom Halves
sections.content:
While an interrupt handler runs, that CPU is not running anything else, and further interrupts of the same kind may be masked. Interrupt handlers also run in **interrupt context**: there is no process to put to sleep, so they can't block, take a sleeping lock, or touch user memory. A slow handler makes the whole machine stutter, so Linux (like every serious kernel) splits device handling in two:

**Top half (the hard IRQ handler).** Runs immediately, with the bare minimum of work: acknowledge the device so it stops asserting the interrupt, grab the status ("which queue entries are done?"), maybe copy out a few bytes that would otherwise be lost, schedule the rest, and return. Ideally that takes microseconds.

**Bottom half (deferred work).** Runs soon after, with interrupts enabled:
- **softirqs**: a fixed set of high-priority deferred handlers (`NET_RX`, `NET_TX`, `BLOCK`, `TIMER`, `RCU`, ...). They run on interrupt exit or in per-CPU `ksoftirqd` threads when there's a flood.
- **threaded IRQs**: the handler body runs in a dedicated kernel thread that can sleep and be prioritised (`request_threaded_irq`). The PREEMPT_RT real-time patches, merged into mainline Linux in 6.12 (2024), make almost all handlers threaded.
- **workqueues**: general-purpose kernel worker threads for anything that needs to sleep. Linux 6.9 added BH workqueues as the successor to the older, now-deprecated *tasklets*.

Networking shows why this matters. At 10 million packets per second, an interrupt per packet would consume the machine (*receive livelock*: 100% CPU spent handling interrupts, nothing processed). Linux's **NAPI** solves this adaptively. The first packet raises an interrupt; the driver **disables further receive interrupts** and schedules a softirq that **polls** the NIC ring for up to a budget of packets (64 by default). Only when the ring is empty does it re-enable interrupts. Under light load you get interrupt-driven low latency; under heavy load you get efficient polling. NICs add **interrupt coalescing** ("raise one interrupt per 50 µs or per 64 packets", tunable with `ethtool -C`), trading a little latency for a lot of throughput.

Practical knobs you may meet in production: `/proc/interrupts` (which CPUs take which IRQs), `irqbalance` or `/proc/irq/N/smp_affinity` (pin a NIC queue's interrupts to specific cores, away from your latency-critical threads), and `/proc/softirqs`.

sections.title: DMA, and Polling vs Interrupts
sections.content:
Early devices used **programmed I/O**: the CPU copied every byte between a device register and memory. That is fine for a keyboard, impossible for a 7 GB/s SSD. **Direct Memory Access (DMA)** lets the device move data itself:

1. The driver allocates buffers and writes **descriptors** into a ring in RAM: "read 128 KB from LBA 4096 into the physical (or IOVA) address 0x1f3a000".
2. It rings a **doorbell**, a write to a device register.
3. The device becomes a **bus master** and transfers data over PCIe directly into RAM. The CPU is free to run other threads.
4. When done, the device writes a **completion entry** and raises an **MSI-X interrupt**. The handler reaps completions and wakes the thread waiting in `read()`.

The **IOMMU** (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, ARM SMMU) sits between devices and RAM, translating device addresses and restricting each device to the buffers it was given. Without it, a malicious Thunderbolt or PCIe device could DMA over kernel memory. DMA is also what makes **zero-copy** possible: `sendfile()` and `splice()` move file data from the page cache to the NIC without copying it through user space (busybox `cat` uses `sendfile`, and nginx does for static files with `sendfile on`).

**Interrupts vs polling** is a latency-vs-efficiency trade-off:
- **Interrupts**: the CPU does nothing until the device signals. That's efficient when events are rare, but each interrupt costs a few microseconds (entry, handler, cache disruption, a wake-up and context switch for the waiting thread).
- **Polling**: the CPU repeatedly checks a completion queue. That burns a core when idle, but when the device answers in under 10 µs (modern NVMe, RDMA, fast NICs), the interrupt overhead can be a large fraction of total latency. Polling wins on latency, and under heavy load it wins on throughput too.

Real systems mix the two: NAPI for networks, **hybrid polling** for NVMe (`io_uring` with `IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL`), socket **busy polling** (`SO_BUSY_POLL`), and full **kernel bypass** (DPDK, SPDK), where a user-space driver owns the device and dedicates whole cores to polling. HFT shops and storage engines do this, at the cost of cores that are always 100% busy.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Thread
    participant K as Kernel / driver
    participant SSD as NVMe SSD
    participant RAM as RAM
    T->>K: read(fd, buf, 128 KB) - page cache miss
    K->>SSD: write descriptor to submission queue, ring doorbell
    K->>K: thread sleeps, scheduler runs other work
    SSD->>RAM: DMA 128 KB directly into page-cache pages
    SSD->>K: completion entry + MSI-X interrupt
    K->>K: top half - ack, note completion, schedule bottom half
    K->>K: bottom half - mark pages up to date, wake thread
    K-->>T: copy page cache to buf, return 131072
sections.caption: A disk read that misses the page cache. The CPU only sets up the transfer and handles one interrupt at the end. The SSD moves the data into RAM by DMA while the waiting thread sleeps and the core runs other work.

sections.title: Blocking vs Non-Blocking I/O
sections.content:
By default, I/O syscalls are **blocking**. `read()` on a socket with no data puts the calling thread to sleep on a wait queue. The scheduler runs something else, and when a packet arrives the interrupt, then the softirq, then the protocol stack wakes the thread. That makes programming simple (code reads top to bottom), and it's how classic servers worked: **one thread (or process) per connection**.

The cost shows up at scale. Ten thousand idle keep-alive connections means ten thousand threads, each with a kernel task, a stack (8 MB of virtual address space by default with glibc, at least a few pages actually used), and scheduler bookkeeping, plus a context switch every time one of them wakes. This was the **C10K problem** (Dan Kegel, 1999). The answer was to stop parking one thread per socket.

**Non-blocking I/O**: set `O_NONBLOCK` on the fd (`fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK)`, or `setblocking(False)` in Python). Now `read()` with no data returns immediately with **`EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK`**, and `write()` to a full socket buffer writes what fits and returns a short count. The thread never sleeps inside an I/O call. But on its own this is useless: you'd spin re-trying every socket. You need a way to ask the kernel *which* fds are ready. That's **I/O multiplexing**, covered next.

Two models of async I/O exist, and the difference matters:
- **Readiness-based** (`select`, `poll`, `epoll`, `kqueue`): the kernel says "fd 7 is readable now." You then make the `read()` call yourself, which won't block.
- **Completion-based** (Windows IOCP, `io_uring`): you say "read into this buffer," and the kernel later says "done, 512 bytes." The data is already in your buffer.

**The regular-file trap**: readiness APIs consider regular files *always ready*. `select`/`poll` report them readable, and `epoll_ctl` refuses them with `EPERM`. But a `read()` that misses the page cache still blocks the thread while the disk works. There has never been a portable, reliable non-blocking `read()` for files. This single fact explains why Node.js uses a thread pool for `fs`, and why `io_uring` was such a big deal.

sections.title: I/O Multiplexing: select, poll, epoll, kqueue
sections.content:
Multiplexing lets **one thread wait on thousands of fds at once** and wake only when at least one is ready. Four generations:

| API | Origin | How it works | Cost per wait | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `select` | 4.2BSD, 1983 | Pass bitmaps of fds; kernel scans them; returns modified bitmaps | O(n) in all fds | Hard limit `FD_SETSIZE` = 1024; bitmaps rebuilt every call |
| `poll` | System V, 1986 | Pass an array of `{fd, events}`; kernel fills `revents` | O(n) in all fds | No 1024 limit, but still copies and scans everything |
| `epoll` | Linux 2.5.44 / 2.6, 2002–03 | Kernel keeps the interest set (red-black tree) and a ready list | O(ready) | `epoll_create1`, `epoll_ctl` once per fd, `epoll_wait` |
| `kqueue` | FreeBSD 4.1, 2000 (also macOS) | `kevent()` both registers changes and waits | O(ready) | Generic: sockets, files changing, processes, signals, timers |

The breakthrough of `epoll` and `kqueue` is that the **interest list lives in the kernel**. With `select`/`poll`, a server with 50,000 mostly idle connections hands the kernel all 50,000 fds on every loop iteration, and the kernel checks all of them, even if only 3 are ready. With `epoll`, you register each fd once. When a packet arrives, the network stack appends that fd to the epoll instance's **ready list** (from the softirq path), and `epoll_wait` just copies out the ready entries.

Two `epoll` modes:
- **Level-triggered** (default): `epoll_wait` keeps reporting the fd while data remains. It's forgiving, and behaves like `poll`.
- **Edge-triggered** (`EPOLLET`): reports only on the *transition* to ready. You **must** read until `EAGAIN`, or the leftover data sits there and you never hear about it again. Faster, easy to get wrong.

Further flags: `EPOLLONESHOT` (disarm after one event, useful when several threads share an epoll fd), and `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` (Linux 4.5, wake only one of the waiters, avoiding the **thundering herd** when many workers wait on one listening socket).

Everything event-driven sits on these APIs: nginx, Redis, HAProxy, Envoy, Netty, Go's netpoller, Python's `asyncio`, Rust's Tokio (via `mio`), and libuv (Node.js). Windows' native model is **IOCP**, which is completion-based. Portable libraries hide the difference behind one interface.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# One thread, many sockets: non-blocking I/O + an OS readiness API.
import selectors, socket

sel = selectors.DefaultSelector()          # epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS/BSD
print("backend:", type(sel).__name__)

# Three "connections" (socketpair = two connected sockets, no network needed)
pairs = [socket.socketpair() for _ in range(3)]
for i, (server_end, _client_end) in enumerate(pairs):
    server_end.setblocking(False)          # sets O_NONBLOCK on the fd
    sel.register(server_end, selectors.EVENT_READ, data=f"conn{i}")

# 1) Non-blocking read with no data: the kernel returns EAGAIN instead of sleeping
try:
    pairs[0][0].recv(1024)
except BlockingIOError as e:
    print("recv on empty socket ->", e.errno, "EAGAIN")   # 11 on Linux, 35 on macOS

# 2) Two clients send; one stays silent
pairs[2][1].send(b"hello from 2")
pairs[0][1].send(b"hello from 0")

# 3) One blocking call asks the kernel: which of my fds are readable?
for key, mask in sel.select(timeout=1.0):  # epoll_wait / kevent under the hood (order may vary)
    msg = key.fileobj.recv(1024)
    print(f"{key.data} ready -> {msg!r}")
    key.fileobj.send(msg.upper())          # echo back

print("conn1 got nothing and cost us nothing while we waited")
print("client 0 receives:", pairs[0][1].recv(1024))
for s, c in pairs:
    sel.unregister(s); s.close(); c.close()
sections.explanation: One thread watches three sockets. `setblocking(False)` sets `O_NONBLOCK`, so reading an empty socket raises `BlockingIOError` (errno `EAGAIN`) instead of sleeping. `selectors.DefaultSelector` picks the best API for the OS (`EpollSelector` on Linux, `KqueueSelector` on macOS). A single `sel.select()` call, which is `epoll_wait`/`kevent` underneath, returns only the two sockets that have data. The silent `conn1` costs nothing while we wait. Output (Linux): `backend: EpollSelector`, `recv on empty socket -> 11 EAGAIN`, then `conn2 ready -> b'hello from 2'` and `conn0 ready -> b'hello from 0'`, then `client 0 receives: b'HELLO FROM 0'`. This loop, scaled up with a callback per fd, is exactly what `asyncio` and libuv are.

sections.title: io_uring: Completion-Based I/O with Shared Rings
sections.content:
`epoll` fixed waiting, but each ready socket still costs at least one syscall to read or write, and regular files still block. **`io_uring`**, added in **Linux 5.1 (2019)** by block-layer maintainer Jens Axboe, rethinks the interface:

- At setup (`io_uring_setup`), the kernel and the process **share two ring buffers through `mmap`**: a **submission queue (SQ)** of request entries (SQEs) and a **completion queue (CQ)** of result entries (CQEs).
- To issue I/O, you write SQEs into the ring: opcode, fd, buffer, length, offset, and an opaque `user_data` tag. That is plain memory writes, no syscall.
- One **`io_uring_enter`** call submits *any number* of queued SQEs, and can also wait for completions in the same call. With **`SQPOLL`**, a kernel thread polls the SQ, so a busy application can submit and reap I/O with **zero syscalls** in steady state.
- Results appear as CQEs `{user_data, res, flags}`. You read them straight from shared memory.

It is truly asynchronous for **files as well as sockets**. Operations include read/write (buffered and `O_DIRECT`), `fsync`, `openat`, `statx`, `accept`, `connect`, `send`/`recv`, timeouts, cancellation, *linked* chains ("write then fsync"), *multishot* accept/recv (one SQE produces many completions), registered buffers and files (skip per-call setup), and zero-copy send and receive. Users include ScyllaDB/Seastar, TigerBeetle, QEMU, RocksDB, and **PostgreSQL 18** (2025), which added asynchronous I/O with `io_method = io_uring` as an option (the default is `worker`).

**The catch is security.** `io_uring` is a large, fast-moving kernel subsystem that bypasses the per-syscall checkpoints that seccomp filters and security tools rely on. Google reported that 60% of the kernel exploits submitted to its 2022 bug bounty used `io_uring`, and disabled it in ChromeOS, for Android apps, and on its production servers. Linux 6.6 added the `kernel.io_uring_disabled` sysctl, and container runtimes' default seccomp profiles (Docker's among them) block it. In practice: excellent for a database or storage engine you control, often unavailable inside locked-down containers.

sections.caption: `io_uring` replaces "one syscall per operation" with two shared ring buffers. The app queues many requests with plain memory writes, submits them all with a single `io_uring_enter` (or none at all with SQPOLL), and collects results from the completion ring. It works for files as well as sockets.

sections.title: How Node.js and libuv Use All of This
sections.content:
Node.js runs your JavaScript on **one thread**, yet serves thousands of concurrent connections. The trick is **libuv**, a C library that wraps each OS's best I/O mechanism:

| Platform | Network I/O | Files, DNS, crypto, zlib |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `epoll` | thread pool |
| macOS / BSD | `kqueue` | thread pool |
| Windows | IOCP (completion-based) | thread pool for most file ops |

**Sockets, pipes, TTYs**: libuv puts every socket in non-blocking mode and registers it with `epoll`/`kqueue`. The heart of each event-loop iteration is the **poll phase**, one `epoll_wait()` (or `kevent()`) whose timeout is "until the next timer is due." When it returns, libuv calls `read()`/`accept()`/`write()` on the ready fds (non-blocking, so they never stall) and runs your JavaScript callbacks. That's why `strace` on an idle Node server shows a thread sitting in `epoll_pwait`.

**Files** can't be done this way (regular files are "always ready"), and neither can `dns.lookup()` (it calls libc's blocking `getaddrinfo()`), CPU-heavy `crypto` (`pbkdf2`, `scrypt`, async `randomBytes`), or `zlib`. libuv sends these to a **thread pool, 4 threads by default** (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, up to 1024). A pool thread makes the ordinary *blocking* syscall, and on completion it wakes the event loop through an `eventfd` (Linux) or a pipe, so your callback runs on the main thread. So `fs.readFile()` isn't non-blocking at the kernel level; it's a blocking `read()` on someone else's thread.

Consequences every Node developer should know:
- **The pool is shared and small.** Four slow NFS reads, or four `bcrypt` hashes, occupy the whole pool, and every `fs` call and `dns.lookup()` (behind `http.get('http://host')`) queues behind them. Raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` (set it before the pool starts, ideally in the environment), use `dns.promises.resolve*()` (c-ares, non-blocking sockets), or move heavy CPU work to `worker_threads`.
- **`*Sync` APIs** (`readFileSync`, `execSync`) make the blocking syscall *on the event-loop thread itself*: no other request is served until it returns.
- **io_uring**: libuv 1.45 (2023) began using `io_uring` for file operations on Linux. After a security issue in early 2024, Node.js turned it **off by default**; it can be enabled with `UV_USE_IO_URING=1`. So on current Node the thread pool still does file I/O.

Python's `asyncio` follows the same pattern, with `selectors` for sockets and `loop.run_in_executor()` / `asyncio.to_thread()` for blocking file work. Go hides it in the runtime: goroutines doing network I/O park on the netpoller (`epoll`/`kqueue`), while a goroutine stuck in a blocking file syscall keeps its OS thread, and the runtime hands its scheduler slot to another thread so the remaining goroutines keep running.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Eight CPU-heavy `pbkdf2` jobs, a pool of four threads. With the default `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4` the jobs finish in **two waves** (on an 8-core laptop: jobs 1–4 at ~180 ms, jobs 5–8 at ~330 ms). With `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8` all eight run in parallel and finish together (~250–310 ms; each is a bit slower because they now compete for cores). The timer fires at ~10–20 ms either way, which shows the event-loop thread stays free while pool threads do the work. Swap `pbkdf2` for `fs.readFile` on a slow network drive, or for `dns.lookup`, and you get the same queueing. It's a common, invisible cause of latency spikes in Node services.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming one `write()` writes everything.** `write()` and `send()` may return a *short count* (full socket buffer, signal interruption, pipe capacity). Loop until all bytes are written, or use a library that does. Likewise `read()` returning fewer bytes than asked is normal, not EOF; only `0` means EOF.
- **Treating `EINTR` and `EAGAIN` as fatal.** `EINTR` means a signal interrupted a blocking call: retry it. `EAGAIN` on a non-blocking fd means "not now": wait for readiness.
- **Edge-triggered epoll without draining.** With `EPOLLET`, if you read only part of the data you won't be notified again, and the connection appears to hang.
- **Using `select()` with fds above 1023.** `FD_SET` on fd 1024+ writes past the bitmap: silent memory corruption, not an error. Use `poll`/`epoll`.
- **Thinking async file I/O is free in Node.** It runs on a 4-thread pool shared with DNS lookups and crypto. Slow disks or network file systems can stall unrelated requests.
- **One syscall per tiny item.** Unbuffered logging, one `write()` per row, one `stat()` per file in a hot path. Batch, buffer, or cache.
- **Leaving `strace` on a production process.** `ptrace` can slow a process by 10–100×. Prefer `perf trace`, `bpftrace`, or `strace -c` on a short-lived test.
- **Calling `*Sync` APIs in a server request path.** `fs.readFileSync`, `child_process.execSync`, and `crypto.pbkdf2Sync` block the only JavaScript thread.

**Your syscall debugging toolkit**: `strace -f -e trace=%file,%network -T` (what is it doing, and how long does each call take?), `strace -c` (what does it do most?), `ltrace` (library calls), `perf trace` and `bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_enter { @[comm] = count(); }'` (low-overhead, safe on production), `/proc/<pid>/stack` and `/proc/<pid>/wchan` (where in the kernel a stuck thread is sleeping), `lsof -p <pid>` and `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd` (what's open), and `cat /proc/interrupts` (where IRQs land). On macOS: `dtruss`, `fs_usage`, and Instruments. When a process "hangs," `strace -p` usually shows you within seconds which syscall it's blocked in.

items: **User mode vs kernel mode** is enforced by the CPU (x86 ring 3 vs ring 0, ARM EL0 vs EL1). User code can't run privileged instructions or touch kernel memory, so every interaction with hardware or other processes must go through the kernel.

A **system call** is a numbered request with arguments in registers, entered with one trapping instruction (`syscall` on x86-64, `svc` on ARM64) to a fixed kernel entry point. The kernel validates the arguments, does the work, and returns a result or `-errno`, which libc turns into `-1` + `errno`.

Syscalls cost roughly **100× a function call** (tens to hundreds of ns, more with Spectre/Meltdown mitigations, plus cache and TLB pollution). **Batch** work (buffers, `writev`, `io_uring`). The **vDSO** runs `clock_gettime`, `gettimeofday`, and (since Linux 6.11) `getrandom` in user space with no kernel entry.

On Linux `fork()` and `pthread_create()` are both **`clone`** with different sharing flags. `open()` is implemented with **`openat`**. **`futex`** keeps uncontended locks in user space. **`strace`** shows every call but slows the target a lot; use `perf trace` or eBPF in production.

**Hardware interrupts** are asynchronous (devices, timer, IPIs). **Exceptions** are synchronous: **faults** retry the instruction (page fault), **traps** continue after it (`int3`), **aborts** are fatal. System calls are deliberate traps.

Interrupt handling is split: a fast **top half** acknowledges the device, and a **bottom half** (softirq, threaded IRQ, workqueue) does the rest. **NAPI** switches NICs from interrupts to polling under load, and **DMA** lets devices copy data into RAM while the CPU does other work.

**Blocking I/O** sleeps the thread. **Non-blocking I/O** (`O_NONBLOCK`) returns `EAGAIN`. **Readiness APIs** (`select` O(n) with a 1024-fd limit, `poll` O(n), `epoll`/`kqueue` O(ready) with a kernel-side interest list) tell you when to retry. **Completion APIs** (IOCP, `io_uring`) do the I/O and report the result.

**Regular files are always 'ready'** to `select`/`poll`/`epoll`, so readiness APIs can't make disk reads non-blocking. That's why libuv uses a thread pool for files, and why **`io_uring`** (Linux 5.1+, shared SQ/CQ rings, batched or zero-syscall submission) matters. It is often disabled in hardened environments for security reasons.

**Node.js/libuv**: sockets use non-blocking fds plus `epoll`/`kqueue`/IOCP on the event-loop thread. `fs`, `dns.lookup`, `crypto.pbkdf2`/`scrypt`, and `zlib` use a **4-thread pool** (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`). `*Sync` APIs block the event loop itself.

quiz.question: Why can't a normal user-space program simply execute an instruction that disables interrupts or loads a new page-table root?
options: The compiler refuses to emit such instructions for user programs
The CPU runs user code at a lower privilege level (ring 3 / EL0), where privileged instructions raise a fault and the kernel handles it
Those instructions only exist on server CPUs
The C standard library intercepts them and returns EPERM
quiz.explanation: Privilege is enforced by the CPU itself. In ring 3 (EL0 on ARM), privileged instructions trigger a general-protection fault, which the kernel handles, typically by killing the process. Compilers and libc have nothing to do with it.

quiz.question: On x86-64 Linux, what does the libc `write()` wrapper do to actually enter the kernel?
options: Calls a kernel function directly through a function pointer exported by the kernel
Sends a message to a kernel daemon process over a Unix socket
Places the syscall number in `rax` and the arguments in registers, then executes the `syscall` instruction, which jumps to a fixed kernel entry point
Raises a page fault on purpose so the kernel's fault handler notices the request
quiz.explanation: A syscall is a numbered request: the number goes in `rax` (1 for `write`), the arguments in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, ..., and `syscall` switches to ring 0 at the address in the `IA32_LSTAR` MSR. User code can never choose an arbitrary kernel address to jump to.

quiz.question: Why does calling `clock_gettime()` (or `performance.now()` in Node) usually NOT enter the kernel on Linux?
options: It is served from the vDSO, a kernel-provided shared library mapped into every process that reads kernel-maintained time data in user space
The CPU caches the result of the last syscall and returns it again
Time functions are implemented by the compiler as constants
glibc keeps a background thread that updates a global variable every nanosecond
quiz.explanation: The vDSO (`linux-vdso.so.1`) contains user-space implementations of `clock_gettime`, `gettimeofday`, `time`, `getcpu`, and (since 6.11) `getrandom`. They read a data page the kernel keeps updated plus the CPU timestamp counter, so no mode switch is needed.

quiz.question: A process accesses a page that is valid but currently not in RAM. The kernel loads it from disk and returns. What happens next?
options: The process receives SIGSEGV because the access failed the first time
Execution continues at the instruction after the load, and the loaded value is lost
The kernel emulates the load instruction in software and skips it
The CPU re-executes the same load instruction, which now succeeds, because a page fault is a *fault*-class exception
quiz.explanation: Faults are reported before the instruction completes, and the CPU restarts that instruction after the handler returns. Traps, like the `int3` breakpoint, resume at the next instruction. Aborts are unrecoverable.

quiz.question: Why do Linux drivers split interrupt handling into a top half and a bottom half?
options: Because the top half runs in user space and the bottom half runs in the kernel
The top half runs immediately in interrupt context, where it can't sleep and delays everything else on that CPU, so it does the minimum and defers the rest to softirqs, threaded IRQs, or workqueues
To let two CPUs process the same interrupt in parallel
Because hardware only allows 50% of an interrupt to be handled at once
quiz.explanation: Hard IRQ handlers must be fast: they run with that interrupt (and sometimes all interrupts) masked and can't block. They acknowledge the device and record status; the heavy work runs later in deferred contexts with interrupts enabled.

quiz.question: What does DMA (Direct Memory Access) change about a disk read?
options: The device transfers the data directly into RAM, and the CPU only sets up descriptors and handles a completion interrupt, instead of copying every byte itself
The CPU reads data directly from the disk platters without involving the controller
The data bypasses RAM and goes straight into the CPU's L1 cache
Disk reads become synchronous and can no longer block the calling thread
quiz.explanation: With DMA the device bus-masters the transfer into memory (through the IOMMU on modern systems) and signals completion with an interrupt. The CPU is free to run other threads while the transfer happens. The calling thread still sleeps until completion.

quiz.question: A server watches 50,000 mostly idle connections, and only a handful are active at any moment. Why does `epoll` scale much better than `poll` here?
options: `epoll` uses multiple CPU cores automatically while `poll` uses one
`poll` is limited to 1024 file descriptors
With `epoll`, the interest set is registered once and kept in the kernel, which maintains a ready list, so each wait costs O(ready fds) instead of passing and scanning all 50,000 fds every call
`epoll` makes reads non-blocking, while `poll` makes them blocking
quiz.explanation: `poll` copies the whole fd array in and out and the kernel checks every entry each call, O(n). `epoll_ctl` registers fds once, the kernel appends fds to a ready list as events occur, and `epoll_wait` returns only those. The 1024 limit belongs to `select`, not `poll`.

quiz.question: You use edge-triggered epoll (`EPOLLET`). A socket becomes readable with 10 KB of data, and you read only 4 KB, then go back to `epoll_wait`. What is the likely result?
options: epoll reports the socket again immediately because 6 KB remain
The kernel discards the remaining 6 KB
epoll_wait returns an error because the buffer was not drained
You may never be notified about the remaining 6 KB, because edge-triggered mode reports only new transitions to readable, so the connection can appear to hang
quiz.explanation: Edge-triggered mode signals changes, not state. The rule is to keep reading until `read()` returns `EAGAIN`. Level-triggered mode (the default) would keep reporting the fd while data remains.

quiz.question: In Node.js, why does `fs.readFile()` use libuv's thread pool, while socket reads use `epoll`/`kqueue` directly?
options: File reads are CPU-bound, while socket reads are I/O-bound
Readiness APIs treat regular files as always ready, so a non-blocking read of a file can still block on disk. libuv performs the blocking read on a pool thread instead
epoll is only available for TCP, not for UDP or files, for licensing reasons
The thread pool is faster than epoll for every kind of I/O
quiz.explanation: `select`/`poll` report regular files as readable, and `epoll_ctl` rejects them with `EPERM`, yet a page-cache miss still blocks. So libuv runs ordinary blocking file syscalls on its pool (4 threads by default) and posts the completion back to the event loop.

quiz.question: What is the key design idea behind `io_uring`?
options: It replaces the kernel's TCP stack with a user-space implementation
It adds a faster version of `select` with no 1024-fd limit
Applications and the kernel share submission and completion ring buffers, so many I/O requests (files and sockets) can be queued with memory writes and submitted with one syscall, or none with SQPOLL
It makes every syscall run in user mode by default
quiz.explanation: `io_uring` (Linux 5.1+) is completion-based: SQEs go into a shared submission ring, `io_uring_enter` submits them in a batch (or an SQPOLL kernel thread picks them up), and results come back as CQEs. Unlike epoll, it handles regular files asynchronously too.
